analysis: A vintage Louis Vuitton Monogram Abbesses messenger bag, $600-800 -- first of a three-lot fashion consignment (1002, 1003, 1004). The Abbesses was produced from the late 1990s, so 'vintage' means about twenty-five years old. Designer handbags are a live secondary market but a completely separate one from antiques, and nothing here touches a criterion.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is above what a used Abbesses makes. Vuitton is also the most counterfeited brand on earth and authentication requires the date code, the hardware, the stitch count and the lining -- none of which is addressed. Coated canvas cracks at the corners and the vachetta handles darken and split.

analysis: A vintage Louis Vuitton Monogram Drouot shoulder bag, $300-500. Second of the fashion consignment; the Drouot ran from the mid-1980s. Same reasoning as 1002.
problems: Same authentication and condition exposure as 1002. Estimate is above the used market.

analysis: Three pieces of 1980s women's designer clothing, $100-200. Catalogued to the decade. Vintage clothing has an audience but no overlap with this collection, and no designer is named.
problems: No designers named, no sizes, no condition. Estimate assumes labels the catalogue does not claim.

analysis: A French P. & Y. Augousti shagreen nautilus tray, $300-500. Augousti is a Paris atelier working in shagreen, parchment and exotic materials since 1990 -- genuinely fine contemporary craft with a design following, and shagreen has an Art Deco lineage. Modern, and no criteria fit.
problems: Post-1926 by six decades. Shagreen -- stingray skin -- is a CITES-listed material in some species and provenance for the skin is not addressed. Contemporary design pieces bought at auction typically resell well below their gallery price.

analysis: A Portuguese blue and white tile plaque, $300-400. Azulejo panels are a genuine and long tradition, and 18th- and 19th-century ones are real antiques with attractive hand-painted line.
problems: No date, no size, no tile count. Portuguese azulejos have been made continuously to the present and modern hand-painted panels are sold as decorative goods throughout Portugal -- the tells are the glaze thickness, the biscuit colour at the edges, and whether the brushwork carries through the cobalt with the tonal variation of hand painting. Also worth confirming the panel was not taken from a building.

analysis: A Victorian needlepoint French-style armchair, $300-500. Genuinely antique in all likelihood, and needlepoint upholstery of the period can be handsome. But this is the exact centre of the weak market the standing brief names -- upholstered Victorian furniture -- and it has not recovered.
problems: Upholstered Victorian seating regularly fails to sell. If the needlepoint is worn, reupholstery costs several times the purchase price; if it is good, it is fragile and cannot be used. 'French style' is the cataloguer declining to commit.

analysis: An oak-framed walking-stick display case, $600-800. A display fitting, not a collection object -- useful if you own the canes in 1025 and 1027, and priced as though it were furniture.
problems: Above the comfortable band at $792-1,056 all-in for a case. No date, no maker. Display cases are made new for the trade.

analysis: Two antique British antler-handled walking canes, $400-600. Catalogued as antique, and staghorn-handled sticks with silver or nickel collars are a genuine Victorian and Edwardian form. Antler is unrestricted material, unlike the ivory-handled sticks elsewhere in this sale. Companion lot to the porcelain-knob canes at 1027.
problems: 'Antique' with no date. Antler handles crack along the grain and the joint to the shaft is where these fail; check both. Silver collars, if present, are mounts with no meaningful metal content. At $528-792 all-in the estimate is mid-to-upper band for two sticks.
patience: High. Cane lots run regularly at Thomaston.

analysis: Eighty-plus California gridiron programmes in remarkable condition, $400-600. College football programmes are a real collecting field and a large run in high grade is genuinely uncommon -- 'remarkable condition' is the whole basis of the estimate and is at least a specific claim. Wrong coast, post-1926, no criteria fit.
problems: No date range, no teams, no landmark games identified -- programme value is entirely about which games. Part of the California consignment pattern the standing brief flags: wrong coast, skip the block.

analysis: The description supplies exactly the evidence I said was missing, and it changes the call. Not 'hand forged copper pans' of no date, but '(4) 19TH C. Copper Pots, probably French, HAND DOVETAILED construction with triple riveted heart shaped handle terminals, traces of original tin lining. One handle marked "41"'. Hand-dovetailed seams are the single tell that separates period French batterie de cuisine from modern spun reproduction, and the catalogue states them. Triple-riveted heart-shaped handle terminals are a French professional-kitchen convention. This is the best of the eight-lot copper block by a distance and the only one with both a date and a construction detail behind it.
problems: Decorative copper is still the weak market the brief names, and that has not changed. The tin lining survives only in traces, so these are decorative rather than usable without retinning at $50-150 a pan. 'Probably French' is the house hedging on origin, though the construction supports it. The '41' on one handle is a size or inventory number, not a maker's mark -- do not read it as one. Four large pans is a lot of wall.
patience: High. French copper runs constantly, but dated and dovetailed sets at $300-500 are the better end of it.

analysis: Four pieces of 19th-century French copper cookware, $300-500 -- and this is the only lot in the copper block with a date attached, which makes it the one where the age criterion is actually met. French batterie de cuisine of the period is heavy-gauge, dovetail-seamed and often stamped with a chateau or hotel mark.
problems: Still the weak market the brief names. Untinned or worn-tinned copper is decorative only. Check for dovetailed seams (period) versus rolled or spun seams (modern reproduction), and for iron rather than brass handles. At $396-660 all-in it is mid-band for four pans.

analysis: A vintage copper stock pot with lid, $200-300. 'Vintage' with no date, in the middle of the copper block.
problems: No date, no maker. Estimate is above the market for a single decorative pot.

analysis: A large copper pot with side handles, $200-300. Copper block, no date, no maker.
problems: Same as 1051.

analysis: A copper and brass countertop beverage dispenser, $200-300. A hotel or soda-fountain fitting; more interesting than a plain pot but still undated.
problems: No date, no maker. Dispensers of this type are reproduced for the decorator and restaurant trade. Missing taps and internal fittings are common.

analysis: Two pieces of Continental copper cookware, $200-300. Copper block, no date, no country beyond 'Continental'.
problems: Same as 1051.

analysis: Five graduated 19th-century brass preserve pans, $500-700. Dated to the century, so genuinely antique, and a graduated nest of five is a display object rather than five pans -- that is what lifts it above the rest of the copper block. Brass preserve pans with iron handles are honest 19th-century kitchen equipment.
problems: At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band. Brass preserve pans are reproduced for the decorator trade and hung on kitchen walls everywhere. Check for hand-riveted iron handles and hammer marks on the interior. Graduated sets are frequently assembled from separate pans -- confirm the nest is genuine.

analysis: A fifteen-piece copper cookware collection, $800-1,200 -- the largest and highest-estimated lot in the copper block. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget for a category the standing brief names as weak. No date, no maker, no tinning condition on fifteen pieces. Buying fifteen pans is a storage decision.

analysis: Hope D. Wagner (Cochrane School, DC), $400-600. 'Cochrane School' with no further attribution is the kind of hopeful label the standing brief warns about -- a school name attached to a name with no auction record. Washington DC, not Maine.
problems: No date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Artist does not index. Estimate assumes the name carries weight.

analysis: Steven Hileman (American, contemporary), $500-700. Catalogued as contemporary, so modern by definition, and a living artist with no established auction market.
problems: No date, no medium, no title. Contemporary work bought at auction generally resells below the artist's own studio prices. Not a criteria fit.

analysis: Two artisan-signed turned wood vessels, $300-500. 'Artisan signed' is the exact phrase the standing brief singles out: the cataloguer saw a signature and could not identify it. Contemporary woodturning.
problems: Unidentified signature, no date, no wood species, no dimensions. Studio woodturning has a thin secondary market. Estimate is a gallery number.

analysis: A 1930-era painted pine figure, $600-800. Catalogued to c.1930, so just outside the antique line but close enough to have real folk-art character. Carved and painted figures of this date are collected as American folk sculpture even when they miss 1926.
problems: Just post-1926, so it earns nothing on the age criterion. No subject, no size, no maker. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band. Painted surface is everything on a folk figure -- confirm it is original rather than refreshed.

analysis: A vintage New York City rotary-dial pay phone, $100-200. Mid-century industrial telephony with a nostalgia audience. The lowest estimate in this group and roughly right for the market.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. Pay phones are heavy and the internal mechanism is usually seized or stripped. No date.

analysis: A brass-bound mahogany humidor, $300-500. Brass-bound campaign-style boxes are a genuine Victorian and Edwardian form and a good humidor with its cedar lining and working lock is an attractive desk object.
problems: No date, no maker. Brass-bound boxes are reproduced heavily -- Indian and Chinese-made 'campaign' boxes are sold new by the thousand and age quickly. The tells are the timber, the hand-cut dovetails and the quality of the lock. Cedar linings crack and humidor hardware is usually replaced.

analysis: A three-piece painted wicker furniture set, $400-600. Painted wicker is a summer-cottage staple in coastal Maine and there is a genuine local audience for it. Undated, and most surviving painted wicker is 1920s-50s.
problems: No date. Wicker is fragile: broken reeds, sprung frames and multiple repaints are the norm, and repainting hides all of it. Three-piece sets are large. Estimate is at the top of the market.
patience: Very high. Painted wicker is in every Maine summer-house sale.

analysis: An Elvis Presley scarf with an unused 18 August 1977 Portland, Maine concert ticket, $300-500. The date is the point: Presley died on 16 August 1977, two days before this concert, so the ticket is for a show that never happened -- which is exactly why it survived unused. That is a genuinely interesting piece of Maine ephemera with a specific and poignant story.
problems: Post-1926 by half a century and no criteria fit. Elvis memorabilia is also heavily faked and the stage-worn-scarf claim in particular is the most abused provenance in the field -- unless the scarf has documentation, treat it as a souvenir scarf. The ticket is the real object here and unused August 1977 tickets do survive in numbers.

analysis: Kenneth Smallwood (20th c. American), $300-500. A 20th-century American artist with no auction record, no date, no medium and no title given.
problems: Name does not index. No information beyond the century. Estimate assumes the name means something.

analysis: Pamela Holeman (Woodbridge, CT), $700-900. Connecticut, contemporary, no auction record. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band as well.
problems: Above budget, unindexed name, no date, no medium, no title. Nothing to assess.

analysis: Jamie Wyeth (American, b. 1946), $300-400 -- the opening lot of the eleven-lot Wyeth block (1162-1172) and the only Jamie rather than Andrew. Jamie Wyeth is a genuine Maine figure with a real market, and Monhegan and Tenants Harbor subjects sell locally. But like every other lot in this consignment, no medium and no process is named, and the pattern established across 1163 (giclee), 1164 (1993 Aaron Ashley reproduction), 1169 (Helga portfolios) and 1166-1171 (matted flush, unsigned) is unambiguous: this is a consignment of reproductions.
problems: No medium, no title, no process, no edition. The room will bid the name. At $300-400 for what is most likely an unsigned reproduction, the estimate is three to six times the object.
patience: Very high. Thirty-seven Wyeth lots across this sale.

analysis: A Singer 'Sew Handy' child-sized sewing machine, $300-400. Child's Singers are genuinely collected and the early cast-iron ones straddle the antique line. A charming small object with a documented maker.
problems: The Sew Handy name covers models from about 1910 to the 1950s, so the date is open and later ones are common and cheap. Value depends on the model number, the finish, and whether the original case and clamp are present -- none stated. Estimate is above the market for the common models.

analysis: A circa 1870s child's riding horse glider, $500-700. Catalogued to the decade, so genuinely antique, and platform gliders -- the horse suspended on a swinging frame rather than rockers -- are a distinct and collected form. A large, handsome object with real presence.
problems: At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band. Riding horses were used hard: expect a replaced mane and tail, a repainted or restored hide, and repairs at the leg joints and the glider mechanism. Original paint and original hide are worth several times a restored example, and 'circa 1870s' is the catalogue's claim rather than evidence.
patience: Moderate. Platform gliders run periodically; original-surface ones are the minority.

analysis: An Ibanez RGA72QM electric guitar, $500-700 -- part of a seven-lot instrument consignment (1214-1224). A current-production Japanese-designed instrument.
problems: Modern, no criteria fit. At $660-924 all-in you are paying above new retail for a used guitar.

analysis: Two British Besson brass marching-band flugelhorns, $300-500. Besson of London is a documented and important brass-instrument maker and their late-19th and early-20th-century instruments are genuinely collected as well as played. The best lot in the instrument consignment on age and maker.
problems: No date, so 'border' rather than antique -- Besson production spans well past 1926 and serial numbers date them. Brass instruments of this age almost always have dents, red-rot in the leadpipe and seized valves; restoration is specialist and expensive. Confirm both are Besson London rather than the later Besson-branded student instruments.

analysis: Two 1960s banjos, one with a case, $300-500. Catalogued to the decade, so post-1926 by four decades. The folk-revival banjos of the 1960s are numerous and mostly student-grade.
problems: No makers named, which is the entire valuation on banjos -- a 1960s Gibson is a different object from a 1960s Kay. No condition information. Estimate assumes names not claimed.

analysis: An Oscar Schmidt OS15B fifteen-chord autoharp, $200-300. A production instrument still in the catalogue.
problems: Modern, no criteria fit. Estimate is at or above what a used OS15B sells for.

analysis: A Fender CD60CE acoustic/electric in a case, $200-300. A current-production entry-level instrument.
problems: Modern, no criteria fit. Estimate is above the used market for a CD60CE.

analysis: A 1920s child-size banjo, unmarked, $200-300. Catalogued to the decade, so it sits right on the 1926 line. Small parlour and child's banjos of the tenor-banjo era are appealing decorative objects.
problems: Unmarked, so no maker premium and no way to date it more precisely than the decade. Old banjos have shrunken heads, warped necks and missing hardware. Estimate is at the top of the market for an unmarked child's instrument.

analysis: Linda English (20th c.), $300-400. A name with no dates, no nationality, no medium and no auction record.
problems: Nothing to assess. Unindexed name, no information beyond the century.

analysis: Avraham Shemi-Shoham (Israel, 1935- ), $250-350. A living Israeli artist, so necessarily post-1926 work, with a thin international auction record.
problems: No date, no medium, no title. Israeli modern art has a market but it is made in Tel Aviv, not Maine. No criteria fit.

analysis: An 18th-century drum-form soldier's canteen, $300-500. Catalogued to the century, which puts it among the small group of genuinely 18th-century objects in this sale, and wooden drum canteens -- coopered staves, iron or wooden hoops, a turned spout -- are the standard soldier's water bottle of the Revolutionary and Colonial periods. A real, used, dateable military object inside the band with room.
problems: Drum canteens are reproduced for reenactment in exactly this form and the reproductions are made the same way from the same materials, so age has to be read from the surface: genuine ones have shrunken staves, dried and split hoops, old iron with layered rust, and dirt worked into the end grain. Painted regimental markings, if any, need particular scepticism -- they are the most commonly added feature. No provenance offered.
patience: Moderate. Coopered canteens appear in Americana sales periodically; period ones are the smaller share.

analysis: Three Remington R293 'Hunter-Trader-Trapper' knives, $200-400. Part of the same Remington collectable-knife consignment as 1245, 1252, 1259, 1262 and 1267 -- six lots of manufactured collectables in one session.
problems: Same as 1245: 1980s-90s collectables with a soft secondary market. Post-1926, no criteria fit.

analysis: A Remington Model 722 in .244 Remington, $300-500. The 722 is a well-made post-war bolt action and .244 Rem is an uncommon chambering, which adds modest collector interest.
problems: Post-1926, modern firearm requiring FFL transfer, no criteria fit. Estimate is roughly the market so there is no bargain.

analysis: A Winchester Model 74 in .22 Short, $200-400. A common semi-automatic rimfire made 1939-1955; the .22 Short-only chambering is the earlier and slightly less common configuration.
problems: Post-1926, FFL transfer, no criteria fit. Estimate is at the top of the market for a Model 74.

analysis: A Mossberg Model 151K in .22 LR, $150-300. A post-war semi-automatic rimfire; the cheapest gun in the consignment and a plain one.
problems: Post-1926, FFL transfer, no criteria fit.

analysis: A RAD hewer with scabbard, $800-1,200 -- the Reichsarbeitsdienst hewer, second of the two Third Reich edged-weapon lots (see 1277). An active collectors' market. Post-1926, above the comfortable band at $1,056-1,584 all-in, and no criteria fit.
problems: Above budget. RAD hewers are extensively reproduced and the fakes have been in the market for decades; maker's mark, blade motto and scabbard fittings all need checking. As with 1277, this is a subject-matter decision for the buyer to make on their own terms.

analysis: A two-piece cultured pearl suite, $400-600. Cultured pearls have been produced commercially since the 1920s and the market for ordinary strands has fallen a long way -- akoya strands that retailed at $2,000 in 1990 sell for $150-400 now.
problems: No date, no metal content on the clasps, no pearl size or quality grading, no length. Without a metal weight there is no melt floor to calculate. Cultured pearl value is almost entirely about lustre and matching, neither of which is described. Estimate is above the current market.

analysis: A pair of walrus tusks and a boar tusk mounted as a bottle opener, $200-300. Walrus is a marine mammal and its ivory is regulated under the Marine Mammal Protection Act; undocumented walrus ivory cannot lawfully be sold in interstate commerce, and several states including Maine restrict it further.
problems: Marine mammal ivory with no documentation of age or origin. Resale is recorded as zero for the same reason as the elephant-ivory lots: whatever it is worth to look at, it cannot be sold on. Do not bid.
patience: Not applicable -- a category to avoid.

analysis: A hand-painted replica of an 18th-century naval battle, $300-500. The catalogue says replica, which settles it -- a modern painting of an old subject.
problems: Catalogued as a replica and estimated at $300-500. No artist, no date. The marine subject is the only appeal and it is a decorative one.

analysis: An RIAA gold record award for 'You Don't Have to Be a Star', $400-500 -- first of a four-lot RIAA award consignment (1323, 1324, 1326, 1327). Presentation awards are a genuine music-memorabilia category and in-house awards presented to the artist or label staff carry real value.
problems: Post-1926 by half a century, no criteria fit. RIAA plaques are also reproduced and sold as decor, and the difference between a period in-house award and a modern replica made from the same components is the float plate, the RIAA hologram or strip-plate style, and the presentation inscription. None is described.

analysis: An RIAA gold record award for 'I Hope We Get to Love in Time' by Marilyn McCoo & Billy Davis Jr., $400-500. Second of the RIAA consignment and a companion to 1323 -- same artists, same year.
problems: Same as 1323.

analysis: An RIAA gold record award for 'Phoenix' by Grand Funk Railroad, $500-700. Third of the RIAA consignment. Grand Funk awards carry more than the McCoo/Davis ones because the band has a larger collecting base.
problems: Same authentication issues as 1323. Post-1926, no criteria fit.

analysis: An RIAA gold record award for 'We're an American Band' by Grand Funk Railroad, $1,000-1,500 -- the best-known title in the RIAA consignment and the highest estimate. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Same authentication issues as 1323, and they matter more at this price: for a well-known title the replica trade is more active, not less.

analysis: A Chinese carved wood figure of Guanyin with a rock, $300-500. Undated, part of the Day 1 Chinese decorative block.
problems: No date, no wood, no size. Carved Guanyin figures are produced continuously in enormous numbers. Religious sculpture provenance questions apply to genuinely old examples, which this is unlikely to be.

analysis: A Chinese Shiwan immortal figure, $200-300 -- the third Shiwan lot in the sale alongside 1337 and 1349. Undated.
problems: Same as 1337 and 1349, and three of them compete in one session.

analysis: A Chinese blanc de chine figure of Bodhidharma on the waves, $200-300. Dehua blanc de chine is a genuine tradition running from the Ming to the present, and the Bodhidharma-crossing-the-river subject is one of its standards -- which means it has been made continuously for four hundred years. Undated.
problems: No date, no mark. Blanc de chine is exceptionally hard to date from a photograph because the body and glaze changed little. Estimate is above the undated market.

analysis: A 'Louis XV French style' armchair, $300-400. 'Style' is the cataloguer declining to commit to a period, and on French furniture that is the whole question -- this is a revival chair, not an 18th-century one.
problems: 'Style' with no date. Upholstered seating in the weak market the standing brief names. Reupholstery costs more than the chair.

analysis: A Randolph and Claudia Laub cloth mat, $300-500. Contemporary textile artists with no established auction record.
problems: Unindexed names, no date, no dimensions, no technique. Contemporary craft textiles have essentially no secondary market.

analysis: A Caplan mid-century beach house scene, $300-400 -- one of three Caplan lots in the sale (1348, 3322, 3323, the last dated '51). A single-name signature with no first name, no dates and no auction record: the standing principle on unidentified signatures applies.
problems: No first name, no dates, no medium, no dimensions. Three lots by the same unidentified hand in one sale, which suggests one consignment of one person's work rather than a market.
patience: Very high -- three in this sale.

analysis: 'Unidentified Israeli artist', $300-400. The catalogue is candid: nobody knows who painted it. Price it as the anonymous work it is.
problems: No artist, no date, no medium, no title. Estimate assumes decorative demand.

analysis: Steve Gianakos (NYC, 1938- ), $300-400. Gianakos is a documented New York artist with gallery representation and a modest auction record -- one of the better-established contemporary names in this section. Post-1926 and no criteria fit.
problems: No date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Contemporary New York work in a Maine general sale rarely finds its audience.

analysis: The description is a delight and a warning at once. The subject is 'Boy and Girl at a Crane Well, in front of a Dutch Colonial cottage with gambrel roof, roaring river with TRUSS BRIDGE in valley to right, oil on canvas, unsigned, in later gold molded frame'. A Dutch Colonial gambrel cottage and a crane well are genuine Hudson Valley vernacular, which supports the upstate New York attribution. The iron truss bridge is a useful dating detail in its own right -- those are a post-1850 form, so this is second-half-of-the-century work rather than early.
problems: 'RELINED AND REPAIRED.' On an unsigned naive painting that is a significant discount: relining flattens the impasto that gives folk painting its character, and 'repaired' unspecified means you must look for inpainting under UV. The frame is described as later, so it adds nothing. Naive paintings are also faked, and a relined canvas is harder to read for age, not easier.
patience: Moderate. Naive American farm views run periodically; good ones with buildings and animals are the better share.

analysis: Mabel Mikel Williams (20th c. American), $300-400. Williams was an illustrator with a modest record; no date, medium or title given.
problems: No information beyond the name and the century. Thin auction record.

analysis: Two Chinese pigskin boxes with a maker's seal, $300-400. Chinese leather trunks and hat boxes with painted and lacquered decoration were export goods and travelling equipment through the late Qing and Republic periods, and a maker's seal is more than most of the Chinese decorative lots here offer.
problems: No date, and the maker's seal is mentioned but not read. Pigskin trunks are also made new. Leather dries and splits; check the hinges, the corners and the interior paper linings, which is where the dates and shop labels usually are.

analysis: A pair of early Thai painted wood home guardian figures, $400-800. Thai guardian figures with original polychrome are genuine folk sculpture and, if actually early, would satisfy the age criterion. The wide estimate band suggests the house is uncertain too.
problems: 'Early' is not a date. Southeast Asian wooden figures are produced in enormous quantity for the export decorative trade and aged convincingly -- the tells are shrinkage cracks running through rather than around the paint, insect damage that has stopped, and old repairs. Religious and household guardian figures also raise export questions from Thailand.

analysis: A pair of Himalayan-style repousse metal religious plaques, $400-600. 'Style' again -- the cataloguer declining to commit. Nepali and Tibetan repousse work is produced continuously in Patan and Kathmandu for both devotional and tourist markets.
problems: 'Style' with no date and no metal identified. Estimate is above the decorative market. Religious material provenance questions.

analysis: Roger Eliot Gilson (20th c. MA), $300-400. A Massachusetts 20th-century painter with no significant auction record.
problems: No date, no medium, no title. Unindexed name.

analysis: 'Woman Picking Berries', $300-400 -- a title with no artist, no date and no medium. An anonymous decorative picture.
problems: Nothing identified. Estimate assumes decorative demand.

analysis: The description names the subject and it is squarely on the Maine criterion: 'MAINE LOBSTERMAN'S HOME, oil on canvas. In whitewashed silver frame, signed lower right.' Not just a generic coastal scene -- a named Maine working subject, and a large canvas at 23 1/2 x 35 1/2 in. At $250-350 for a signed Maine oil of that size, inside the band, this is a reasonable wall picture even though the hand behind it is unidentified.
problems: 'Coan' is a surname with no first name, no dates and no auction record -- the standing principle on unidentified signatures applies and there is no maker premium here. Modern, so nothing on the age criterion; it earns its place on regional subject alone, which should be said plainly. A whitewashed silver frame is a decorator's choice and may want replacing. Deep supply: Maine lobstering subjects are the single most painted theme in the state.

analysis: Renee Berger (early 20th c. NY), $300-500. An early-20th-century New York painter, so the work straddles the antique line, but with no auction record and nothing else stated.
problems: No date, no medium, no title. Unindexed name. Wrong region.

analysis: 'Unidentified early 20th c. Danish artist', $300-500. Candid cataloguing: no artist. Danish painting of the period is competent and abundant.
problems: No artist, no date, no medium, no title. Straddles the antique line with no way to tell. Price as the anonymous decorative picture it is.

analysis: Two vintage wooden Coca-Cola crates, $100-200. Advertising crates are the entry level of breweriana and soda collecting.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. Estimate is two to three times the market -- wooden Coke crates sell for $15-40 each. Reproduced heavily for decor.

analysis: Marco Alquinga (Ecuador, 20th c.), $200-400. An Ecuadorian 20th-century painter with no auction record in the American market.
problems: No date, no medium, no title. Unindexed name, wrong hemisphere for this collection.

analysis: A copper plaque with repousse classical figures, $200-300. Decorative copper again -- the weak market the standing brief names -- with a classical subject that has been reproduced since the Renaissance.
problems: No date, no maker, no size. Repousse classical plaques are produced continuously for the decorative trade. Estimate is above the market.

analysis: 'Unidentified mid-century Peruvian artist', $1,000-1,500 -- the highest estimate in the sale attached to an explicitly unidentified artist. That combination is worth pausing on: the house has put four figures on a painting it cannot attribute, which means the estimate rests entirely on how the picture looks.
problems: Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in for an anonymous work. No date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Nothing here is checkable.

analysis: An unsigned nude study, $400-600. Unsigned, undated, no medium. Academic nude studies span two centuries and are hard to date without the sheet in hand.
problems: Nothing identified. If it is a genuine 19th-century academy study it is worth the estimate; if it is a 1970s life-class drawing it is worth $50. Nothing in the catalogue distinguishes them.

analysis: Marjorie Moore (Maine/American, b. 1944), 'Flight', 1992, $400-600 -- one of two Moore lots (see 3329). A living Maine artist, dated to the year, and the Maine criterion is explicitly about regional desirability rather than age. But Moore's auction record is thin and 1992 is recent.
problems: Post-1926 by sixty-six years. No medium or dimensions. Two lots by the same living artist in one sale compete with each other. Living-artist work bought at auction rarely resells above what the artist charges.

analysis: Rebecca Goodale (Maine/American, b. 1965), 'Bear', 2003, $300-400 -- one of two Goodale lots (see 1463). Goodale is a Portland-based book artist working on Maine's endangered species, which is genuinely regional and genuinely interesting work. Dated to the year and firmly contemporary.
problems: Post-1926 by many decades; the Maine criterion is about regional desirability, and Goodale's market is small and largely institutional -- her work is in library and museum collections rather than at auction. No medium or format stated, which matters because her artist's books and her prints are different objects.

analysis: Rebecca Goodale (Maine/American, b. 1965), 'Turtle', 2005, $300-400. Companion to 1462, two years later. Same reasoning.
problems: Same as 1462, and competing with it.

analysis: F. Hochstein (Berkeley artist), abstract cityscape, 1964, $300-500. Dated to the year, and part of the California consignment pattern the standing brief identifies -- wrong coast, no criteria fit, skip the block rather than analysing each.
problems: Post-1926. Unindexed name with only an initial. California mid-century abstraction is a large and largely anonymous supply.

analysis: Six hand-painted school posters of 'racial types', circa 1880, $400-600. Catalogued to c.1880, so genuinely antique, and 19th-century schoolroom wall charts are a real category with a design following -- large, graphic, hand-coloured teaching aids.
problems: The subject is the difficulty and it should be stated plainly: these are 19th-century racial-typology charts, produced to teach a pseudoscience that was used to justify colonialism and worse. They have historical value as documents of how that thinking was taught, and museums collect them for exactly that reason, but they are not decorative objects and hanging them is a different decision from buying them. Beyond that: large paper on canvas or rollers, usually varnished, cracked and torn at the edges.

analysis: A 1745 Zurich Bible in an ornate leather binding, with 1759 calligraphy, $500-700. Two dates, both catalogued: the printing in 1745 and an added calligraphic inscription in 1759, which is family-record material and is exactly the kind of documentation that lifts a common text into a specific object. Swiss Reformation Bibles of this date in original bindings are handsome, heavy, and genuinely 280 years old. Inside the band at $660-924 all-in.
problems: The condition line is worse than I assumed and it is all in the binding, which is where I said the value was: 'Damages to pastedown, contents generally good. WORMAGE TO BINDING, BRONZE PLACKET FROM BACK COVER GONE.' So the tooled full calf has worm and the back cover has lost one of its brass fittings -- on a binding with brass corners, hasps and a five-banded spine, a missing placket is conspicuous. The contents are the sound part. Note also that the calligraphy leaf is dated 1759 and there is a further 1779 inscription inside the back endpaper, so the book carries three dates across four decades, which is genuinely good provenance for a family Bible.

analysis: A framed 'Conn. Bank Note List and City of Hartford Monthly Advertiser', $200-300. Bank note reporters -- periodicals listing which banks' notes were good and at what discount -- are a vivid artefact of the pre-national-currency era and genuinely antique. A specific, dateable, useful document.
problems: Framed, so the date, the issue number and the reverse cannot be seen. Newsprint of this period is acidic and light-struck; assume browning. Ephemera has a shallow resale market. Estimate is at the top of what these make.

analysis: 'Railroad Routes in California, 1853', $100-200 -- the cheapest antique in this section. Dated to the year, genuinely 173 years old, and the 1853 Pacific Railroad Survey period is a specific and collected moment in American cartography. Wrong coast for this collection, but the price is right.
problems: Wrong region and no criteria fit beyond age. Probably an extracted plate from a report, so expect fold lines and offsetting. No publisher or engraver named.

analysis: A Danish royal appointment signed by the King and Queen, 1976, $200-300. Dated to the year -- and Denmark had no King in 1976. Margrethe II acceded in 1972; her consort was Prince Henrik, never King. Either the document is not what it is described as, or the description is careless.
problems: The description is factually impossible as written, which is worth flagging alongside the other cataloguing errors in this sale. Post-1926, no criteria fit. Royal appointment documents are also produced in quantity by chanceries and are usually secretarially signed.
